Tomato___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small, water-soaked, dark brown to black spots on leaves, often surrounded by a yellow halo. Advanced stages cause leaf drop and fruit spotting.
advice: Avoid overhead watering; use drip irrigation or water at the base of the plant to keep leaves dry.
Remove and safely destroy severely infected lower leaves and plant debris (do not compost).
Sanitize pruning tools and stakes between plants using a dilute bleach or alcohol solution.
Practice a 2-3 year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops (avoid planting after peppers, potatoes, or eggplants).
Consult your local agricultural extension office or authorized plant clinic for region-approved copper-based bactericides or bio-control agents if disease pressure is high.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.disclaimer: Always consult a local agricultural extension officer or certified agronomist before applying chemical treatments.

Tomato___Early_blight.symptoms: Brown to black spots with concentric rings (target-like pattern), usually starting on older, lower leaves. Leaves turn yellow around spots and drop prematurely.
advice: Prune and dispose of infected lower foliage to reduce splashing of fungal spores from the soil.
Apply organic mulch (straw, dried grass) around the plant base to create a physical barrier preventing soil splash onto foliage.
Space plants adequately to ensure good air circulation and sunlight penetration.
Avoid working in the field when foliage is wet.
Consult your local agriculture officer or university extension service regarding recommended protective bio-fungicides or copper sprays.
Tomato___Early_blight.disclaimer: Always consult a local agricultural extension officer or certified agronomist before applying chemical treatments.

Tomato___Late_blight.symptoms: Large, irregular, water-soaked dark lesions on leaves and stems. White, fuzzy fungal-like growth may appear on the undersides of leaves in humid or cool conditions.
advice: Late blight is aggressive and spreads rapidly in cool, humid weather; monitor plants daily.
Immediately isolate or remove infected plants and bag them securely for disposal (burn or bury deeply away from crops).
Do not compost infected plant parts as spores can survive and spread.
Ensure proper row spacing and avoid overhead irrigation to keep foliage dry.
Contact your local agriculture extension department immediately for community-wide alerts and approved preventive fungicides.
Tomato___Late_blight.disclaimer: Always consult a local agricultural extension officer or certified agronomist before applying chemical treatments.

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.symptoms: Pale greenish-yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces; olive-green or grayish velvety mold on the underside of corresponding areas. Common in greenhouses and high humidity.
advice: Improve air circulation and ventilation around plants by pruning excess suckers and widening plant spacing.
Reduce relative humidity below 85% if growing in greenhouses, polyhouses, or tunnels.
Water early in the morning and at ground level so foliage dries quickly.
Sanitize greenhouse structures, tools, and stakes at the end of the season.
Seek guidance from a local agriculture expert for suitable registered fungicides if persistent.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.disclaimer: Always consult a local agricultural extension officer or certified agronomist before applying chemical treatments.

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.symptoms: Numerous small, circular spots with dark brown margins and sunken grayish or tan centers. Tiny black specks (pycnidia) can often be seen inside the spots.
advice: Remove and destroy infected bottom leaves as soon as first spots appear.
Mulch heavily around tomato plants to stop fungal spores from splashing up from contaminated soil.
Avoid overhead watering and do not touch or prune plants when wet.
Rotate crops every 2-3 years away from nightshades.
Discuss appropriate fungicidal spray schedules with a local agricultural extension advisor.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.disclaimer: Always consult a local agricultural extension officer or certified agronomist before applying chemical treatments.

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.symptoms: Fine yellow or white stippling (tiny dots) on upper leaf surfaces. Leaves may turn bronze or dry out. Fine silken webbing can be observed on leaf undersides and shoot tips.
advice: Spray the undersides of leaves with a strong jet of clean water to dislodge mites and disrupt webs.
In hot and dry conditions, apply insecticidal soap or neem oil spray thoroughly covering the leaf undersides in late afternoon.
Encourage beneficial predatory mites or predatory lady beetles in the field.
Avoid excessive synthetic nitrogen fertilizers, which promote rapid, tender growth favored by spider mites.
Consult your local agricultural extension service for integrated pest management (IPM) recommendations.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.disclaimer: Always consult a local agricultural extension officer or certified agronomist before applying chemical treatments.

Tomato___Target_Spot.symptoms: Small, pinpoint brown spots on leaves that expand into circular brown lesions with distinct concentric rings and yellow halos.
advice: Maintain wide plant spacing and prune lower leaves to promote rapid drying of foliage.
Use drip irrigation to prevent moisture accumulation on canopy leaves.
Clear fallen leaves and plant debris from beds at regular intervals.
Rotate away from susceptible crops such as peppers, cucumbers, and tomatoes.
Consult local agricultural extension specialists for approved protectant fungicide choices.
Tomato___Target_Spot.disclaimer: Always consult a local agricultural extension officer or certified agronomist before applying chemical treatments.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.symptoms: Severe upward curling and cupping of leaflets, marked yellowing (chlorosis) of leaf margins, stunted bushy growth, and severe blossom drop.
advice: Manage whitefly vectors using yellow sticky traps, insect exclusion netting, or reflective silver mulches.
Carefully pull up and bag severely stunted, infected plants immediately to prevent whiteflies from vectoring the virus to healthy plants.
Spray neem oil or organic insecticidal soap targeting whitefly populations under leaf surfaces.
Choose certified TYLCV-resistant or tolerant tomato varieties for future planting seasons.
Contact your local agricultural extension officer for regional whitefly monitoring and containment protocols.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.disclaimer: Always consult a local agricultural extension officer or certified agronomist before applying chemical treatments.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.symptoms: Mottled light and dark green patterns (mosaic) on foliage, leaf distortion or shoestringing, and stunted plant vigor.
advice: ToMV spreads mechanically on hands, clothing, tools, and pruning shears; wash hands and disinfect tools thoroughly before handling plants.
Smokers or tobacco users should wash hands with soap and water before entering fields, as tobacco products can harbor related viruses.
Carefully rogue (remove and destroy) infected plants to prevent transmission across neighboring plants.
Select certified virus-free seeds and virus-resistant tomato cultivars for your next planting.
Consult your local agricultural department for testing kits or confirmation if extensive spread is suspected.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.disclaimer: Always consult a local agricultural extension officer or certified agronomist before applying chemical treatments.

Tomato___healthy.symptoms: Uniform green leaf texture, no noticeable lesions, spots, yellowing, or abnormal curling.
advice: Continue standard good agricultural practices: balanced fertilization and consistent drip irrigation.
Scout your crop weekly by inspecting both upper and lower leaf surfaces for early signs of pests or disease.
Maintain proper weed management around crop borders to prevent insect vectors from harboring nearby.
Keep records of weather patterns (high humidity or rainfall) to anticipate disease pressure proactively.
Tomato___healthy.disclaimer: Regularly consult local agricultural extension resources for seasonal crop care schedules.

advice: Isolate affected plants if feasible to prevent spread to adjacent crops.
Avoid overhead irrigation and keep foliage dry to limit fungal and bacterial pathogen spread.
Sanitize tools and wash hands before moving to healthy sections of the field.
Take a clear sample or high-resolution photograph to your local agricultural extension service or certified crop advisor for exact identification and treatment options.
